chunks: As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man who misses the Maghrib prayer until the time of ʿIshāʾ arrives. He said: If the time of ʿIshāʾ has arrived and he remembers that he owes the Maghrib prayer, then if he wishes he may begin with Maghrib, and if he wishes he may begin with ʿIshāʾ, then pray Maghrib after it.

So this is an anomalous report, contrary to all the reports, because practice is based on what we have stated previously: that when the time is ample, one should begin with the missed prayer, and when the time is constrained, one begins with the current prayer. There is no time here in which a person is truly given a choice. It is possible that this report may be understood as indicating permissibility, while the earlier reports indicate merit and recommendation.

key_terms.الْجَوَازِ: mere permissibility in acting one way
key_terms.الْفَضْلِ: greater merit or superiority of one option
key_terms.الْمَغْرِبُ: the Maghrib prayer that was missed
key_terms.خَبَرٌ شَاذٌّ: an anomalous report that conflicts with stronger narrations

ai.seo_question: If someone misses Maghrib until ʿIshāʾ time enters, should he pray the missed prayer first or the current one?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the ruling for someone who missed Maghrib and then the time of ʿIshāʾ enters. The apparent wording allows either order, but the compiler explains that this report is anomalous and that the operative ruling is to begin with the missed prayer when time is ample, and with the current prayer when time is tight. He also reconciles the report by interpreting it as indicating permissibility, while other reports indicate what is more virtuous and recommended.
